labelChirho: come to know, learn, find out
descriptionChirho: To come to know a fact, learn information, or find out about a situation through inquiry or experience; focuses on the acquisition of knowledge rather than the recognition of a person. Used of Jesus knowing thoughts (Mark 2:8; 5:30; Luke 5:22), Theophilus knowing the certainty of what he was taught (Luke 1:4), the sinful woman learning where Jesus was dining (Luke 7:37), Paul learning a man was a Roman citizen (Acts 22:24, 29), the tribune seeking to learn the charges (Acts 23:28; 24:8, 11), Agrippa knowing Paul's life (Acts 25:10), learning the island's name was Malta (Acts 28:1), and knowing God's righteous decree (Rom 1:32). Multilingual glosses consistently use cognitive knowledge terms: arb: علم/عرف (know/learn), deu: erkennen (discern), heb: ידע (know), hin: जानना (know), kor: 알다 (know), spa: conocer/saber (know).

To recognize or identify a person or thing by sight, perceiving who or what someone is; a perceptual act of identification rather than abstract knowledge acquisition. Used of recognizing Jesus (Matt 14:35; Mark 6:33, 54), recognizing false prophets by their fruits (Matt 7:16, 20), the disciples recognizing Elijah's identity in John the Baptist (Matt 17:12), the people recognizing Zechariah had seen a vision (Luke 1:22), the Emmaus disciples recognizing Jesus at bread-breaking (Luke 24:16, 31), Rhoda recognizing Peter's voice (Acts 12:14), recognizing Paul was Jewish (Acts 19:34), sailors not recognizing the land (Acts 27:39), and the Corinthians recognizing Paul's authority (2 Cor 1:13). Multilingual glosses emphasize perceptual recognition: arb: عرفوه (they recognized him), heb: הכיר (recognize), hin: पहचानना (identify), kor: 알아보다 (recognize/spot), spa: reconocer (recognize).

To know thoroughly, completely, or with full understanding; the ἐπι- prefix intensifies the root γινώσκω to indicate comprehensive or profound knowledge. Used of the mutual knowledge between the Father and the Son — 'no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son' (Matt 11:27 x2) — and of eschatological full knowledge: 'then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known' (1 Cor 13:12). Multilingual glosses reflect fullness: eng: knows fully / I will know fully, heb: מכיר / אדע בשלמות (recognize / I will know in completeness), hin: पूर्ण जानूँगा (I will know fully), kor: 완전히 알리라 (will know completely), spa: conoce / conoceré plenamente (know / will know fully). This intensive sense goes beyond mere recognition to indicate exhaustive, intimate knowledge.

Passive voice: to be known or recognized by others; the subject is the object of another's knowledge or perception. Used in 1 Cor 13:12 where Paul says he was 'fully known' (by God) even as he will one day fully know, and in 2 Cor 6:9 where the apostles are described as 'unknown yet being recognized' — a paradox of their public ministry. Multilingual glosses confirm the passive: arb: عُرفت (I was known), eng: I was known fully / being recognized, heb: נודעתי / מוכרים (I was known / recognized ones), hin: पूर्ण जाना गया / पहचाने जाते हुए (fully known / being recognized), kor: 알려졌듯이/ 알려진 (as was known / being known), spa: fui conocido plenamente / siendo reconocidos (I was fully known / being recognized). This passive usage is a distinct grammatical and semantic category from the active senses.

To acknowledge or accept something as true, authoritative, or valid; a volitional act of recognition that goes beyond mere cognition to include acceptance and submission to what is recognized. Used of acknowledging that what Paul writes is a command of the Lord (1 Cor 14:37) and of the Corinthians being urged to acknowledge Stephanas' household for their service (1 Cor 16:18). Multilingual glosses show the volitional dimension: arb: ليعرف / فاعرفوا (let him know / recognize them!), deu: erkennen (recognize/acknowledge), heb: יכיר / הכירו (let him acknowledge / acknowledge!), hin: पहचाने / पहचानो (let him recognize / recognize!), kor: 인정할지니 / 인정하라 (let him acknowledge / acknowledge!), spa: reconozca / reconoced (let him acknowledge / acknowledge!). The imperative mood in both occurrences reinforces the volitional, active dimension of this sense.
